clue.text: Fruit, damaged, began to be put in lorries

indicators.note: the scrambled fodder is placed inside the word lorries, between its second and third letters
damaged letters are knocked out of shape, so the word began is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone loading a fruit crop finds it bruised in the trucks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' looks like it describes the fruit, but it is the anagram signal for 'began'; 'to be put in' sets the result between the second and third letters of 'lorries'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hybrid of raspberry and blackberry, these are soft berries, a kind of fruit.

clue.text: We own the chemistry room in the works

parts.note: a lab is a laboratory, a room for chemistry
what we own is ours

explanation.surface: A factory's staff claim the chemistry lab as theirs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' looks like a factory but is the definition, a noun meaning toils.
explanation.definitionFit: Toils and efforts, as in the twelve tasks of Hercules, are one's works.

clue.text: Note to girl which causes reflection

parts.note: G is a note of the musical scale
lass is a word for girl

explanation.surface: A thoughtful message to a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirror throws back an image, and looking in one shows your reflection.

clue.text: It was realized after an early fruit course

definitions.text: It was realized after an early fruit course

parts.words: It was realized after an early fruit course
parts.note: in Genesis Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit and then become aware they are unclothed

explanation.surface: Something sinks in after a starter of fruit at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an early fruit course' reads as a meal's first course, but it is the first fruit ever eaten in Eden.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unclothed was what Adam and Eve noticed once they had eaten the apple.

clue.text: Always the same even if poets remove five

definitions.text: the same even if poets remove five

explanation.surface: A rule that stays fixed whatever poets cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Poets write E'ER for the word: drop the V (Roman five) and the word still means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are forever: the plain word and the poets' shortened form without its Roman five.

clue.text: Reticent after a fault.?

explanation.surface: Someone goes quiet after making a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis a fault is a bad serve, after which the player serves again; read as RE-SERVED.
explanation.definitionFit: Quiet and self-restrained describes a shy person; a tennis server who faults is served again.

clue.text: Supplementing the family — outside for example

indicators.note: outside says the abbreviation for for example goes round the word for the family

parts.note: kin are one's family

explanation.surface: Relatives being shown as an example of extra help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts E and G around KIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out is to stretch a scant supply by adding to it.

clue.text: Case of an extremely important rising in Lincoln

indicators.note: in puts the reversed word inside the president's short name

parts.note: Abe is the short name of Abraham Lincoln

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: vital means extremely important

explanation.surface: A matter of great weight comes up in the city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lincoln' looks like the English city but is the American president, by his short first name. In a down clue 'rising' reads the word backwards, and 'in' puts it inside the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical case of Latin nouns expressing by, with or from.

clue.text: Famous black mare? That's the girl !

definitions.text: Famous black mare? That's the girl !

parts.words: Famous black mare? That's the girl !
parts.note: the highwayman Dick Turpin's horse was Black Bess, and a pet form of that name is how you would cheer her on

explanation.surface: A rider praises a celebrated dark horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Black Bess was the mare of the English highwayman Dick Turpin; the familiar form of her name with -ie is what one would call her fondly.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet form of Elizabeth, the name of Turpin's famous mare made affectionate.

clue.text: De-bagged coal-miners might well be, or have, these

definitions.text: De-bagged coal-miners might well be, or have, these

parts.words: De-bagged coal-miners might well be, or have, these
parts.note: miners stripped of their trousers show sooty limbs, and miners also face strike-breakers who work on during a strike

explanation.surface: Pit workers pranked by having their trousers pulled off.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'de-bag' is British slang for pulling someone's trousers off; a coal-miner's bare shins would be grimy. In British labour slang the same word means a worker who breaks a strike, which miners might be or might have to deal with.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty-shinned legs and strike-breaking workers are the two senses the clue plays on.

clue.text: Inspire one doctor to go to high-class quarter

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification
U is the old British label for upper-class usage
E, east, is one of the four compass quarters

explanation.surface: A medical man is encouraged to move to a posh district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarter' looks like a district of town but gives a compass point, E.
explanation.definitionFit: To instil a feeling or quality in someone is to fill them with it, much as inspiring does.

clue.text: Topsy-turvy promotion team relegated

parts.note: a promoted team goes up a division
a side is a team in sport
a relegated team goes down a division

explanation.surface: A football club goes up one season and down the next, turning everything on its head.
explanation.definitionFit: Topsy-turvy describes things in a muddled, inverted state, with top and bottom swapped.

clue.text: Plans for weights'

parts.note: pro is Latin for for, as in pros and cons
grams are units of weight

explanation.surface: A gym-goer draws up schedules for weightlifting.
explanation.definitionFit: Schedules or planned sets of actions, in the American spelling.

clue.text: Kind of Smith to give cash

explanation.surface: Someone named Smith is asked to pay up.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S makes 'Smith' look like a surname, but it is a metalworker: a silversmith.
explanation.definitionFit: A silversmith works the white precious metal; loose change coins are called by the metal's name.

clue.text: Does a soldier hear it after catching it ?

definitions.text: Does a soldier hear it after catching it ?

parts.words: Does a soldier hear it after catching it ?
parts.note: to catch it is slang for being killed, and a bugle call is sounded at a soldier's funeral

explanation.surface: A question about whether a trooper listens after being punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching it' reads as getting into trouble, but it means being killed; the bugle call at the end of the day is also played at military funerals, when the soldier cannot hear it.
explanation.definitionFit: The bugle call sounded at military funerals and at nightfall in camp.

clue.text: " Then dreams he of another "(R&J)

parts.note: a line from Mercutio's Queen Mab speech in Romeo and Juliet about a sleeping parson, with the last word missing

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Queen Mab speech Mab tickles a parson's nose as he sleeps, and he dreams of another church living to add to the one he holds.
explanation.definitionFit: The parson dreams of a second church post with its income, an ecclesiastical living.

clue.text: Try for Averno, due to change

indicators.note: to change tells us the letters of Averno, due are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller heads for Lake Averno, the classical gate of hell, as plans shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' rearranges AVERNODUE. Averno is a crater lake near Naples.
explanation.definitionFit: An attempt or effort is a try, the noun sense used here.

clue.text: Suggestive of financial assistance in accommodation cost

indicators.note: in places the state handout inside the housing payment

parts.note: rent is what one pays for accommodation
the dole is British unemployment benefit

explanation.surface: Housing benefit wrapped into the rent bill.
explanation.walkthrough: The dole is the everyday British name for unemployment benefit, which here sits inside the payment for accommodation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that evokes or calls to mind another thing is suggestive of it.

clue.text: Stopped when Tess died, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone wrong, so the letters of Tess died are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Something halted at the sad death of Hardy's heroine Tess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges the letters of TESS DIED.
explanation.definitionFit: To desist is to cease or leave off doing something.

clue.text: Condescends to be 23's subjects, it is said

indicators.note: it is said tells us the word for the subjects is only heard, and the entry is spelt differently

parts.note: the monarch at 23 across ruled Denmark, so his subjects were Danes

explanation.surface: Royal subjects are rumoured to lower themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The king at 23 across was Danish, so his subjects are DANES, which sounds like the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To stoop to do something one thinks beneath one is to condescend.

clue.text: Turn to a PR issue, in short

explanation.surface: Someone's attention shifts to a publicity matter.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to direct attention to a subject; as a noun it is the clipped word for a commercial notice.

clue.text: Beautiful and golden, if unreal, in a beautiful golden frame

definitions.text: Beautiful and golden, if unreal, in a beautiful golden frame

parts.words: Beautiful and golden, if unreal, in a beautiful golden frame
parts.note: the golden locks of a portrait, lovely even if painted, framing a face as a gilt frame holds a picture

explanation.surface: A description of a painting in a gilded frame.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'frame' looks like a picture frame, but it is long hair framing a face; 'if unreal' allows dyed or false hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Long locks of hair frame a face as a frame surrounds a painting.

clue.text: I am after gold-this phony type also ?

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm
post is Latin for after, as in postwar
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A gold-digger admits his aim and says he is a fraud too.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a confession by a gold-digger; the clue's own 'I am ... this' points to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraud who pretends to be someone else is a phony sort of person.

clue.text: Rigid -in a bearskin ? (sound idea)

explanation.surface: Someone stiff inside a guardsman's fur hat.
explanation.walkthrough: '(sound idea)' says to hear 'bearskin' as 'bare skin': someone with bare skin is stark naked. A bearskin is also the tall fur cap of British guardsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff or stark rigid; and stark naked, wearing nothing but one's bare skin.

clue.text: Impossibly prohibitive monarch

parts.note: the Danish king of England who, in the legend, set his throne on the shore and forbade the tide to come in

explanation.surface: A king makes bans no one could obey.
explanation.walkthrough: In legend the eleventh-century king of England, Denmark and Norway ordered the sea not to wet him, to show his courtiers the limits of royal power.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary king who forbade the incoming tide issued a ban nobody could enforce.

clue.text: Jack's wedding.

explanation.surface: A man named Jack gets married.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a man's name but is the British flag, the Union Jack.
explanation.definitionFit: The Union Jack is the UK flag; a marriage is a joining of two people.

clue.text: See 11
Shelter a girl

parts.note: a nest is a snug home or shelter

explanation.surface: An instruction to give a young woman a roof over her head.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, used here as an example of a girl.

clue.text: Some coin 'e maybe used for savings

indicators.note: maybe says the letters of some coin 'e could be ordered another way

explanation.surface: A Cockney talks of a few coins he might put by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges SOMECOINE; the apostrophe in 'e is a dropped h and gives just E.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuts in spending and the money they keep back are thrift.

clue.text: Places where. Mr 'Winkle would not' cut a dashing figure ?

definitions.text: Places where. Mr 'Winkle would not' cut a dashing figure ?

parts.words: Places where. Mr 'Winkle would not' cut a dashing figure ?
parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers Mr Winkle makes a fool of himself on the ice, and cutting figures is what skaters do

explanation.surface: Venues where a clumsy Dickens character would look a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Nathaniel Winkle claims to skate but flails on the frozen pond at Dingley Dell; 'cut a figure' is both to look impressive and to trace a figure on ice.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice arenas are where people trace figures on blades, which Winkle could not do.
